draft.title: Perceptions of youth and adulthood
card: A perception is how a person or group sees or understands something. People do not all agree on what it means to be young or to be an adult.
Age is one measure. In Australia, the law treats people as adults at 18, but many people feel like adults earlier or later than that.
Other signs can also mark adulthood, such as living independently, earning an income, finishing study or taking on family responsibilities.
Cultures and families differ in what they expect. Some mark the move to adulthood with a ceremony or a new role in the community, and others by a milestone such as leaving home.
draft.remember: Being young or an adult is seen in different ways, and age is only one of them.

a.q: Which statement best explains why people disagree about when someone becomes an adult?
opts: People and cultures use different signs, not only age
Adulthood is set by law and people misread the law
Physical growth stops at a different age for everyone
Only older people are able to decide who is an adult
a.why: Perceptions of adulthood rest on signs such as independence, work and cultural roles as well as age. The law sets 18 for legal purposes, but it does not settle how people see adulthood, so the option about misreading the law is wrong.
a.clue: Think about signs of adulthood other than a birthday.

b.q: Aisha is 19 and lives with her parents while she studies. Her cousin Tom is 17, has left home and works full time. Which view of adulthood does Tom's family most likely hold?
opts: Independence and work can show adulthood before 18
Adulthood begins only when a person turns 18
Adulthood depends only on finishing school
Living with parents is what makes someone an adult
b.why: Tom's family may see his job and independent living as signs of adulthood, even though he is under 18. The option about turning 18 is tempting because it is the legal age, but perceptions of adulthood go beyond age alone.
b.clue: Look at what Tom has done, not how old he is.

a.best: People and cultures use different signs, not only age

b.best: Independence and work can show adulthood before 18

problems.detail: The scenario says nothing about Tom's family or what they think. Asking which view Tom's family 'most likely' holds makes students guess at an unstated belief. Better to ask which view of adulthood Tom's situation best fits.
The right option is the only hedged one ('can'). The three distractors are all absolute ('is what makes', 'only', 'only'), so a test-wise student could pick it without knowing the idea.
